article_text:
«Utopia? No, grazie». L’idea che i maestri dell’architettura dispensino pillole di saggezza come piacerebbero a noi non supera quasi mai la prova delle interviste. Succede anche con Sir Peter Cook : parli al progettista britannico che negli anni Sessanta fondò Archigram , contribuendo a liberare l’architettura dalla dittatura degli edifici immobili e immaginando città che camminano, e, quando gli chiedi perché abbiamo smesso di coltivare il sogno, risponde sostanzialmente che preferisce parlare d’altro. Il che ha qualcosa di bizzarro, se pensiamo che siamo a Torino, a Utopian Hours, il festival dedicato al futuro delle città che lo ha invitato a tenere una masterclass, mentre una mostra dei suoi disegni, The City is a Garden , a cura di Claudia Pasquero ed ecoLogicStudio, ne celebra l’immaginazione.

Cook, soprannominato all’epoca con i colleghi di Archigram il Beatles dell’architettura radicale, a ottobre ha compiuto novant’anni. E ha poca voglia di farsi trasformare in un monumento all’utopia. Preferisce parlare di progetti, di problemi, di soluzioni. E di quello che accade quando le idee incontrano la forza di gravità.

Il cappello e la città impossibile per Peter Cook

Per esempio, The Line, la città lineare lunga 170 chilometri immaginata nel deserto saudita nell’ambito del progetto Neom, il gigantesco esperimento urbanistico che prometteva di rivoluzionare l’idea stessa di abitare. Cook è stato coinvolto nella progettazione, insieme a molti altri architetti di fama internazionale. «A Londra ci hanno lavorato praticamente tutti», scherza. A lui è toccato studiare una parte residenziale, ragionando sulla frammentazione delle unità abitative e sulla loro distribuzione lungo due fronti. Il problema era integrare gli edifici nel paesaggio, racconta, rispettando al tempo stesso la richiesta di svilupparli molto in altezza, su sezioni estremamente strette. Una combinazione che produceva difficoltà strutturali enormi. Gli chiedo se fosse sbagliata l’idea di partenza o se lo fosse perché tecnicamente irrealizzabile. Cook risponde con un gesto. Si tocca il cappello, se lo sistema sulla testa e spiega che, se qualcuno gli chiedesse di portarlo sempre più in alto, arriverebbe un momento in cui non potrebbe più indossarlo. L’architettura funziona allo stesso modo: puoi spingere una forma oltre ogni convenzione, ma devi ancora poterla usare. Una lezione sorprendente, pronunciata da un uomo che ha passato la vita a disegnare città impossibili. E che ricorda come The Line sia stata presentata anche a Venezia. «Ma pure Venezia è surreale», aggiunge, lasciando aperta una questione: quali impossibilità siamo disposti ad accettare, e perché?

Visionari, con i piedi per terra

Gli chiedo allora che cosa significhi essere visionari. La risposta è fulminea: «Io, noi siamo visionari!». Subito dopo arriva la precisazione che vale l’intera conversazione: la visionarietà deve integrarsi nella realtà. Anzi, aggrapparcisi. Meglio questo che l’utopia, parola sufficientemente elastica da consentire a chiunque di immaginare qualsiasi cosa senza doversi preoccupare troppo delle conseguenze. Cook non sembra avere molta pazienza con l’utopia quando diventa un lasciapassare per ignorare i vincoli del mondo reale. Gli interessa una visionarietà capace di spingere la realtà oltre i propri limiti senza perdere il contatto con la possibilità di costruire. Come ha spiegato di recente, le architetture che immagina sono «possibili, o quasi possibili, ma soprattutto non deliberatamente impossibili».

Ripensando ad Archigram, il ragionamento acquista un significato particolare. La celebre Plug-In City del 1964, con le sue unità intercambiabili, nasceva da una domanda concretissima: perché gli edifici devono durare più delle esigenze di chi li abita? Dietro le immagini fantascientifiche, c’era una critica al funzionalismo e alla rigidità della città moderna. Il futuro serviva a interrogare il presente.

Il diritto di giocare

Nella masterclass presso La Centrale Lavazza, location della decima edizione del festival torinese del citymaking, Cook organizza la propria esperienza attraverso una griglia di temi: paesaggio, città, interni, padiglioni. Quest’ultima categoria gli è particolarmente cara. Il padiglione è il territorio del gioco, della sperimentazione, della libertà di tentare qualcosa senza l’obbligo di trasformarlo immediatamente in modello universale. A novant’anni, Cook continua a considerare il gioco un formidabile motore dell’architettura.

Da oltre sessant’anni affida al disegno il compito di esplorare territori nei quali l’architettura costruita fatica ad avventurarsi. Disegnare gli permette di mettere insieme ciò che nella realtà tende a rimanere separato, di forzare le proporzioni, inventare geografie e studiare le conseguenze di un’intuizione. «Il mio lavoro riguarda l’immaginazione che gioca», racconta. Nei suoi disegni convivono elementi belli, inquietanti e questioni architettoniche estremamente serie, spesso accostati in modi imprevedibili. Compaiono città attraversate da strutture monumentali, edifici che sembrano crescere come organismi, case nascoste nei pendii, paesaggi nei quali vegetazione e costruzioni si contendono lo spazio. Il disegno conserva per Cook una libertà che il rendering fotorealistico tende a sacrificare: può mostrare qualcosa che ancora non esiste senza dover fingere che sia già stato costruito. Lui dice di no, ma a noi piace pensare che sia la nuova, ennesima utopia.

“ Love Actually ” might be one of the most beloved — if controversial — Christmas classics, but don’t try quoting the film to star Keira Knightley. The actress recently revealed that she actually hasn’t watched the film in decades, so interactions with fans who reference her lines mean “nothing” to her.

“I have not watched ‘Love Actually’ since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” she told Heart . “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody. I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting ‘Love Actually,’ but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.”

While filming, Knightley was just 17 and on set for only a week, which contributed to her inability to recall the script. “It was a week when I was 17, so I don’t remember it really,” she continued. “I mean, I quite like that it has this life, this, such a big life out there.”

In the 2003 film, Knightley plays Juliet, a woman who gets married only to learn that her husband’s best friend is actually in love with her. In a now infamous scene, the friend appears at her door and confesses his feelings using cue cards. The cards read: “Let me say, without any hope or agenda, just because it’s Christmas (and at Christmas you tell the truth) to me you are perfect.”

In 2024, Knightley described the moment as “quite creepy” in an interview with the Los Angeles Times. “The slightly stalker-ish aspect of it — I do remember that,” Knightley said. “My memory is of [director] Richard [Curtis], who is now a very dear friend, of me doing the scene, and him going, ‘No, you’re looking at [Lincoln] like he’s creepy,’ and I’m like, ‘But it is quite creepy.’ And then having to redo it to fix my face to make him seem not creepy.”

When asked if she felt there was a creep factor to the scene while filming it, Knightley responded: “I mean, there was a creep factor at the time, right? Also, I knew I was 17. It only seems like a few years ago that everybody else realized I was 17.”

News

National Gallery Singapore to Welcome Chng Hak-Peng as New CEO

CHNG HAK-PENG . Courtesy National Gallery Singapore.

The National Gallery of Singapore (NGS) and Singapore Art Museum (SAM) announced today that Chng Hak-Peng will succeed Eugene Tan as chief executive officer of NGS, effective from January 1, 2027. Tan will step back from his NGS duties at the end of the year to concentrate on his role as SAM’s chief executive officer and director.

Chng brings over 30 years’ experience in Singapore’s arts and culture sector. From 2014 to 2022, he served first as deputy chair, then as chief executive officer, of the Singapore Symphony Group; under his leadership, the Singapore Symphony Orchestra was awarded third place in Gramophone magazine’s Orchestra of the Year 2021, the only Asian orchestra among the nominees. Prior, he spent a decade at the management consultancy Bain & Company. He currently serves on the boards of Library and Archives Solutions, a subsidiary of Singapore’s National Library Board, and Duke-NUS Medical School, and chairs the advisory council of Chua Chu Kang Secondary School. Chng is a PhD candidate in history at the National University of Singapore as well as a long-time volunteer docent for local institutions such as the Asian Civilizations Museum.

In a press release, Chng described the appointment as an opportunity to continue “making the arts accessible and meaningful to our communities . . . [and] to strengthen the role that the arts play in our society.” NGS chairman Peter Ho welcomed the appointment, stating that Chng’s “record of transforming the beloved ensembles of the Singapore Symphony Group speaks for itself,” and that they are “confident the Gallery is in good hands as it continues to grow its voice for Singapore and Southeast Asian art.”

Tan has held the role of NGS director since 2013 and took on the directorship of SAM in 2019. He was appointed CEO of both institutions in 2024. In stepping back from the NGS, Tan said he was “grateful to have had the privilege of leading both NGS and SAM,” and that this is “the right time for each to benefit from dedicated leadership.”

The joint statement framed the split as reflecting “the continued development of both institutions as they enter a new phase of growth,” while noting the two museums will remain “natural partners” that continue to work closely in promoting and showcasing art and culture from Singapore and beyond.

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.

article_text:
In need of a couple’s costume this Halloween? Try a calico apron over a dark dress, a low bun with one loose strand, a cameo broach at your throat; dress a partner in overalls and wire-rimmed glasses, holding a three-pronged pitchfork. It won’t take much to be immediately recognizable as the duo from American Gothic , Grant Wood’s 1930 painting and subject of Wanda Corn’s new book, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon. Why, Corn wants to know, did this painting become so iconic?

Corn, an eminent scholar of American art, has been thinking about this question for five decades. The painting intersected with her own trajectory as an art historian and with her personal history as a descendent of the Midwest: the book includes a photograph of her grandparents posed side-by-side at their home in Indiana, her grandfather in denim overalls, and her grandmother with hair pulled back and a homemade dress. The parallels between the family photograph and American Gothic show how thoroughly Wood, himself raised in Iowa, was tapping in to regional Midwestern identity. Yet a portrait of a midwestern couple is hardly a promising candidate for global fame.

Of course, the pair in American Gothic aren’t a couple, at least not in Wood’s view. He claimed to have intended the twosome to represent a small-town father and daughter, basing the figures on his sister Nan and his dentist. When he made the painting, Wood was searching for a way of working that would be distinctive to the Midwest. He’d tried his hand at French Impressionism, taking several trips to Paris, and worked as a decorator back home in Cedar Rapids. Growing support for the arts in small town America, funded by philanthropists including the Carnegie Foundation, created more opportunities for Wood to make work that felt characteristic of his region.

American Gothic marked Wood’s embrace of a new style as an Iowa painter, developing a pictorial language suited to the visual culture of the Midwest. Rather than straightforward realism, Corn shows American Gothic to be the product of a thorough engagement with pattern and form. Vertical lines, from the tines of the pitchfork to the church steeple in the background, organize and order the composition. Round and oval forms—the figures’ long faces, the woman’s brooch, the pattern on the calico, the shape of the man’s ears—create harmony within the scene. Wood identified what he called a “decorative” quality in his subject matter, basic geometries and hard lines that he translated into paint with such precision that the work was taken to be self-evident rather than deeply thought.

The painting was immediately misunderstood. After winning a prize in a juried exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago, American Gothic —which reproduced well in newsprint thanks to those straightforward, geometric forms—became a sensation. Labeled by the press as a farmer and his wife, the depiction of the couple found detractors in both Iowans and art critics. Locals saw the pitchfork as outdated—four tines would have been more appropriate—and the woman unforgivably dour. Critics couldn’t place the work, finding it out of step with modernist abstraction. Everyone agreed it was an image of marriage.

For Corn, this misunderstanding is key to the painting’s success, allowing for endless adaptation of the archetypal form of two figures joined in union. She traces the painting’s influence in both art and popular culture, drawing on a personal archive of hundreds of reappropriations of the work: American Gothics in butter at a state fair, gay American Gothics in support of same-sex marriage, feminist American Gothics showing the woman heading off to work. Surprisingly, for a painting often dismissed as conservative and reactionary, some of the first adopters of its form were Black urban artists who saw the painting in Chicago in the 1930s. (The Art Institute acquired the painting soon after it debuted.) Certain African American artists saw in Wood a model for a self-taught artist from farm country. Reproducing the motif of a couple posed before a family home became a way of telling stories about migration for artists like Walter Ellison.

Corn’s explanation for American Gothic’s popularity is that it shows the archetype of marriage, a motif that can be traced from Egyptian princes to Etruscan terra cottas to Dutch golden age portraits, rendered in an accessible manner for the modern era. Yet unlike those other examples, beneath the smooth surface of Wood’s painting is a felt unease, a tension that animates the painting and motivates its adaptation. Wood, likely gay, experienced his own failed marriage five years after painting American Gothic. If his aesthetic was one of plainspoken values, he was also singularly able to capture all that goes unsaid when, as is so often the case, reality strains against the expectations of form.

article_text:
田中久貴による写真展「大廈 The Buildings, Mansions.」が、2026年10月13日から18日まで大阪・心斎橋のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。

タイトルの「大廈」とは、中国語でビルや大きな建物を意味する言葉。本作で田中が向き合ったのは、2025年8月の香港だ。地下鉄やトラムを乗り継ぎ、高温多湿の街を歩きながら、建て増しと積層を繰り返す高層住宅や、その窓から突き出すエアコンの室外機、ベランダのない窓辺に干された洗濯物など、都市に刻まれた日常の光景を撮影した。かつて香港のイメージを形づくっていた無数のネオンサインは減少し、九龍寨城は公園となり、啓徳空港もすでに閉鎖されている。田中がカメラを向けるのは、そうした過去の香港へのノスタルジーというより、変貌を続ける都市の現在だ。隙間なく林立する巨大な集合住宅を見上げながら、そのスケールとは裏腹に感じられる「せせこましさ」や、建築の表面から漏れ出す生活の痕跡をモノクロームの画面へと取り込んでいく。

田中はステートメントで、大廈から「冷徹な眼で凝視」される感覚について記している。都市を一方的に観察するのではなく、自らもまた都市から見返される存在として身を置き、そこへ飛び込んでくる「日常としての香港」を受け入れる。その視線の往復から、建築物そのものだけでなく、そこに暮らす人々の存在や時間が浮かび上がる。

本作は2026年、文芸社「写真集大賞」で最優秀賞を受賞。同名写真集『大廈』として9月15日に刊行された。本展では写真集に収められた作品から16点を展示する。

article_text:
In dem mexikanischen Film „ Moscas – Fliegen und andere Gäste “ wird eine einsame alte Frau mit einem kleinen Jungen konfrontiert, der ihren schroffen Panzer, den sie sich über die Jahre zugelegt hat, in Frage stellt. Auf der diesjährigen Berlinale wurde das in Schwarz-weiß gedrehte Drama mit dem Preis der Ökumenischen Jury ausgezeichnet. Ein Gespräch mit dem Regisseur Fernando Eimbcke über die Kunst, die Schwere des Lebens mit dem Zauber und der Unschuld der Kindheit zu verbinden.

In „Moscas - Fliegen und andere Gäste“ geht es um Menschen, die in finanzielle Schieflagen geraten sind. Inwieweit sollen sich Filme mit der politischen Wirklichkeit auseinandersetzen?

Fernando Eimbcke : Das ist eine Entscheidung jedes einzelnen Filmemachers. Man kann sagen, dass Filme immer politisch sind, allein schon durch die Kameraposition, wie Jean-Luc Godard das gesagt hat. Ich bin gegen vieles, was gerade passiert, nicht nur gegen den Krieg in Gaza oder in der Ukraine, sondern auch gegen das, was ICE in den Vereinigten Staaten anstellt, oder was in Mexiko geschieht, wo so viele Menschen verschwinden und zahllose Femizide passieren. Die Liste ist sehr lang. Wie sich diese Themen aber in Filmen wiederfinden, hängt von den einzelnen Filmemachern und Filmemacherinnen ab.

Ihr Film erzählt von einem kleinen Jungen und seinem Vater. Auf welche filmischen Vorbilder haben sie dabei zurückgegriffen?

Eimbcke : Ganz wichtig war „ The Kid “ (1921) von Charlie Chaplin. Chaplin ist eines der größten Genies der Filmgeschichte. Er hat mich als Filmemacher sehr beeinflusst. Chaplin schafft es immer wieder, zwei sehr unterschiedliche Genres zu verschmelzen: das Drama und die Komödie. Auf der einen Seite gibt es diese dramatische Übersteigerung in seinen Filmen, in der eigentlich alle Figuren nur noch Opfer sind; auf der anderen Seite findet sich ein brachialer Humor, bei dem Sahnetorten in die Gesichter klatschen. Chaplin hat mich in all meinen Filmen geprägt, besonders in „ Temporada de Patos “ (2004) oder „ Olmo “ (2025).

Aber auch der italienische Neorealismus hat mit Filmen wie „ Fahrraddiebe “ (1948) von Vittorio De Sica tiefe Spuren bei mir hinterlassen. „Fahrraddiebe“ zeigt die Welt, wie sie wirklich ist. Es ist ein Drama, aber der Grundton ist dennoch realistisch, daher auch der Begriff Neorealismus. Ich glaube, wenn man sich beim Erzählen auf die Wirklichkeit stützen kann, ist das eine sehr starke Basis. Aber man muss sich dieser Wirklichkeit öffnen, sich ihr anpassen und darf nicht versuchen, die Wirklichkeit an sich anzupassen.

Wie haben Sie diese Einflüsse von Chaplin und dem italienischen Neorealismus in Ihre eigene Filmsprache übersetzt?

Eimbcke : Gemeinsam mit der Drehbuchautorin Vanesa Garnica habe ich den Spannungsbogen für „Moscas“ entwickelt. Mit der Bildgestalterin Maria Secco musste ich dann eine Herangehensweise finden, um diese Wirklichkeit visuell und narrativ einzufangen. Das war eine der größten, aber auch schönsten Erfahrungen. Wir ließen die Straße einfach so leben, wie sie lebte. Wir haben nicht auffällig gefilmt, Straßen gesperrt und Lastwagen aufgestellt, sondern die Kamera versteckt angebracht; wir waren dabei sehr diskret und haben nur mit einem sehr kleinen Filmteam gearbeitet. Die Menschen gingen einfach weiter ihren Weg, und das Leben nahm seinen Lauf. Meine Filme „ Club Sandwich “ und auch „ Temporada de Patos “ spielten in abgeschlossenen, isolierten Räumen; „Temporada de Patos“ in einer Wohnung, „Club Sandwich“ in einem Hotel. Bei „Moscas“ wollten wir auf die Straße hinaus, hinein in die Wirklichkeit, und der kindlichen Hauptfigur in diese Umgebung folgen.

Der italienische Neorealismus entstand nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg aus einer Notlage heraus, weil es keine Studios mehr gab. Heute wird viel häufiger im Studio gedreht. Welche Vorteile oder Nachteile hat es, auf der Straße oder in einem Krankenhaus zu drehen?

Eimbcke : Mich hat immer der japanische Regisseur Yasujirō Ozu beeindruckt, insbesondere mit seinem Film „ Erzählungen eines Nachbarn “ (1947), in dem es ebenfalls um eine Frau geht, die sich um ein Kind kümmern muss. Ozu hat meine Arbeit bei den Innenaufnahmen stark beeinflusst. Allerdings drehte er nur ungern im Freien, da er dort das Gefühl hatte, die Kontrolle über die Inszenierung zu verlieren. Bei „Moscas“ verfolge ich bewusst einen entgegengesetzten Ansatz. Ich wollte auf der Straße drehen, um die Kontrolle ein Stück weit aufzugeben. Die Innenwelt hingegen haben wir so gezeigt, wie es auch Ozu getan hat.

Wir haben in einem Krankenhaus gedreht, allerdings nicht in den sensiblen Bereichen. Dort gibt es Menschen, die leiden. Da kann man nicht laut „Kamera läuft!“ rufen. Tatsächlich haben wir das Krankenhaus bis ins Detail studiert und wollten wissen, wie alles aussieht und funktioniert – die Maschinenräume ebenso wie die Krankenzimmer. Unsere Leitfrage war dabei: Wie müssen wir uns anpassen, damit wir es wie gewünscht darstellen können?

Dieser Realismus beinhaltet auch eine starke soziale Komponente. Inwiefern spiegelt der Film die soziale Situation in Mexiko wider?

Eimbcke : Im Zentrum von „Moscas“ stets die Geschichte des Jungen. Deshalb bleibt die Kamera konsequent auf seiner Augenhöhe und nimmt durchgehend seine Perspektive ein. Wir wollten ihn weder belächeln noch als „armes Kind“ rührselig darstellen. Durch diesen Blickwinkel erhalten viele Aspekte der Geschichte eine soziale Dimension. Das zeigt sich beispielsweise am Umgang mit Geld: Die Kamera ist so positioniert, dass der Junge im Bild bleibt und das Geld zwischen ihm und der Kamera auftaucht. Es ließ sich also gar nicht vermeiden, es zu zeigen. Dabei wurde mir bewusst, wie wichtig Geld tatsächlich ist. Man kann zwar behaupten, dass Geld für das Glück keine Rolle spielt. Doch gerade in Krisensituationen oder unter prekären Lebensbedingungen wird deutlich, dass es eben doch eine entscheidende Rolle spielt.

Vanessa Garnica wusste beim Schreiben des Drehbuchs genau, wie viel jedes einzelne Medikament kostet, wie viel Geld der Vater zahlen muss und wie viel er erhalten soll. Auch dadurch vermittelt die Kamera eine gesellschaftliche Stellungnahme. Der Film sagt aber nicht: „Okay, lasst uns über diese Ungerechtigkeit sprechen.“ Es ging darum, die Geschichte eines Kindes zu erzählen.

Was bedeutet es für Sie als Filmemacher, den Film in Schwarz-weißen-Bildern zu entwickeln?

Eimbcke : Wenn man eine Kamera aufstellt, entscheidet man, was man von der Realität zeigen möchte. Mit der Position der Kamera bezieht man einen Standpunkt. Dasselbe gilt für Schwarz-Weiß: Es schafft ein Gleichgewicht zwischen dem Melodram und einer skurrilen Slapstick-Komödie. Wir wurden dabei stark von mexikanischen Fotografen beeinflusst. Wenn über Mexiko gesprochen wird, geht es zu Recht oft um die Farben. Doch viele wichtige Momente der mexikanischen Geschichte wurden in Schwarz-Weiß festgehalten. Fotografen wie Manuel Álvarez Bravo , Graciela Iturbide und Juan Rulfo waren wichtige Bezugspunkte für uns. Außerdem war die Kamerafrau María Secco überzeugt, dass Schwarz-weiß die Unschuld eines Kindes besser einfängt.

Sehr interessant ist, dass sich die Figuren oft gegen die Klischees verhalten, insbesondere die Figur der alten Frau. Wie haben sie diese Figuren entwickelt?

Eimbcke : Die Schauspielerin Teresita Sánchez macht als Olga im Laufe des Films eine Wandlung durch. Ich hatte sie in den Filmen „ La camarista “ (2018) und „ Tótem “ (2023) gesehen. Sie hat dieses mädchenhafte Strahlen. Die Herausforderung in „Moscas“ bestand darin, einen Panzer um diesen kindlichen Kern zu legen. Teresita Sánchez hat intensiv an dieser Schutzhülle gearbeitet. Dadurch wirkt es umso natürlicher, wenn sie ihren inneren Panzer ablegt und das Mädchen wieder zum Vorschein kommt. In der Szene, als sie mit dem Kind ins Krankenhaus geht, um die Mutter des Jungen zu besuchen, laufen beide gemeinsam den langen Flur entlang. In ihren medizinischen Schutzanzügen sehen sie wie zwei Astronauten aus. Schon da wird deutlich, dass sie sich auf das Spiel des Jungen einlassen wird. Wenn sie dann am Automaten ein Videospiel spielen, wird sie wieder zum kleinen Mädchen.

Bei Bastián Escobar , der den Jungen spielt, war diese kindliche Freude ganz selbstverständlich. Unsere Aufgabe bestand darin, seine Unschuld, Spontaneität und seinen Zauber so weit wie möglich zu bewahren und nicht zu verändern. Wir mussten alles darum herum so gestalten, dass sich diese Unschuld, dieses Leuchten und diese Lebendigkeit entfalten konnten. Wir haben nicht viel mehr getan, als zu beobachten und ihn nicht zu stören.

Diese Haltung prägt auch die Inszenierung des Films.

Eimbcke : Genauso verhält es sich auch mit der Kameraführung: Sie darf das Geschehen nicht stören. Man erzählt einfach eine Geschichte in ihrem natürlichen Umfeld und nutzt die Kamera, um diese Geschichte einzufangen. Die Frage ist dabei, wie man möglichst wenig stört. Ich glaube, dass große kommerzielle Produktionen diesen Ansatz tatsächlich behindern. Bei Filmen mit großen Budgets, in denen Kinder mitspielen, habe ich oft den Eindruck, dass sie unterschätzt werden und die Inszenierung ihre Magie und Unbefangenheit beeinträchtigt. Am Ende werden sie so dargestellt, wie es der jeweiligen Geschichte dient. In „Moscas“ ist das anders. Hier passen wir uns dem Kind an.

article_text:
The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize has announced the four shortlisted artists for its 2027 edition. The selected artists are Hoda Afshar , Lotus L. Kang , Sasha Kurmaz and Salvatore Vitale .

Established in 1996 by The Photographers’ Gallery, London, and partnered with the Deutsche Börse group since 2005, the prize recognises artists for an exhibition or book that has made a ‘significant contribution to photography’ in the past year. Previous winners include Rene Matić , Lindokuhle Sobekwa , Lebohang Kganye and Samuel Fosso .

This year’s jury comprises Laia Abril, multidisciplinary artist; Damarice Amao, associate curator for photography at the Musée National d’Art Moderne / Centre Pompidou, Paris; Verónica Fieiras, artist, editor and publisher (CHACO); Anne-Marie Beckmann, Director of Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation and Shoair Mavlian, Director of The Photographers’ Gallery, as voting chair.

‘From century-old photographic archives to radical contemporary experiments, the 2027 shortlist proves how urgently photography speaks to our times. The nominated projects are both rigorous and profoundly moving’, said Beckmann in a statement.

Work by the four selected artists will be on view at The Photographers’ Gallery from 10 March – 6 June.

The winner of the £30,000 prize will be announced in April. The remaining shortlisted artists will each receive £5,000.

Explore the shortlist:

Hoda Afshar

Hoda Afshar is shortlisted for the exhibition Performing the Invisible that took place at the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, Paris from 30 September 2025 to 25 January 2026. Through photographs, drawings, mirrors, videos and sound installations, she explores notions of established perspectives and photography as a tool of resistance. In particular in her series The Fold , she examines the legacy of colonial photographic practice and how they continue to shape the way veiled Islamic bodies are perceived.

Lotus L. Kang

Lotus L. Kang is selected for her exhibition The face of desire is loss , on view at the Bulgari Pavilion at the Venice Biennale through 22 November. Kang considers how bodies change over time. In her work, she suspends lengths of unfixed photographic film from steel joists, displaying how they react to their environment.

Sasha Kurmaz

S asha Kurmaz is recognised for the publication Red Horse published by Éditions Images Vevey in November 2025. The 800-page publication, started in 2022 following Russia’s fullscale invasion of Ukraine, is a visual diary composed of handmade collages that recount the constant reshaping of life in Ukraine by war.

Salvatore Vitale

S alvatore Vitale is shortlisted for the exhibition SABOTAGE that took place at Photo Elysée, Lausanne from 6 March to 31 May. Vitale makes visible the hidden human labour that sustains the digital economy and uses the notion of sabotage to explore the possibility of resistance and agency within systems of control.

Raza, the zodiacal visions of Arpita Singh, illustrated manuscript folios from medieval India and much more, the exhibition traverses artistic landscapes to trace how we used to think of our relationship and responsibility to the world and where we stand now.

Tactile experiences encourage visitors to engage through touch, texture, and material. article_text:
Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming.

That is the main takeaway from a report issued on Wed. by Italian TV producers’ association APA during Rome’s MIA market, which is dedicated to international TV series, animation, feature films and documentaries.

Related Stories

Belgian Series 'The Inheritance' Scores Sony Pictures Television Award at Rome’s MIA Market

After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates which remained firmly in place.

“This situation hinders producers’ ability to plan, increases financial burdens, and shrinks profit margins,” the report pointed out. “It negatively impacts all companies — especially smaller ones — by straining liquidity and limiting their capacity for future investment,” is added. Hopefully, there is some relief in sight with the new tax credit now in place. The so-called application “window” to apply has been reopened.

The report underlined that unscripted content remains the backbone of Italian broadcasting programming, with an output of over 17,000 hours of original, first-run content, being churned out by Italian producers last year. Independent production accounts for 59% of these titles. Unscripted offerings from streaming platforms in Italy have also expanded, with a 51% increase in the number of titles and a 30% rise in total hours.

Within Italy’s unscripted sphere, the factual genre has seen the most significant growth, up 36% in terms of number of hours, with the number of domestic factual titles adapted from international formats doubling. Game shows are also gaining ground on linear networks, both in early evening and prime time slots.

As for scripted originals, the number of titles in 2025 grew 9% to a total 101 shows produced for the current season. But this growth is driven primarily by 74 smaller domestic series for linear networks, that don’t tend to travel, while the number of Italian originals served up by streamers last year stands the same as 2024 with 27 titles, most of which are, similarly, “local for local” product.

The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighbourhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.”

The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “ The Monster of Florence ,” pictured above, directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025.

Meanwhile, as in the rest of the world, the market share for linear television (both free-to-air and pay-TV) is steadily shrinking in Italy while global platforms continue to grow. The streaming segment, which accounted for 21% of the market in 2020, has now reached 43% in the Italian market and “is set to surpass linear television in value in the short-to-medium term,” the report said.

Also in line with global TV trends, microdramas are starting to gain traction in Italy with ReelShort, DramaBox, NetShort, and DramaWave already among the country’s top fifteen entertainment apps in terms of user spend, the report said. And the first original Italian microdrama production has been released, titled “Tutto in una notte,” produced by Fascino PGT, with its 54 episodes distributed on Italian platform WittyTV and on social media.

Thanks to the generosity of a sibling, the New York Public Library (NYPL) is now the owner of some 250 prints by Kiki Smith . They come as the gift of her sister, fellow artist Seton Smith , who has pledged to give all future prints she receives by Kiki to the institution.

The library’s Prints and Spencer Collections already have 30 other Smith prints and 12 of her artist’s books, and with the new gift, including works from as far back as the 1990s and into the present, the library will have one of the most concentrated holdings of the artist’s printed oeuvre in the United States.

“I am very thrilled by my sister Seton Smith’s gift to the New York Public Library because I could think of no more wonderful place for my prints to be,” said Kiki Smith in press materials. “Public libraries are to be cherished.”

The daughter of sculptor Tony Smith, Kiki Smith is a major art historical figure, represented by international gallery Pace, whose founder, Arne Glimcher, mounted a show of her work at his 125 Newbury Gallery in New York just this year. Jan Avgikos wrote in Artforum that in one part of the show, “Smith’s meditations on life and temporality were threaded with wonder at the ineffability of the natural world,” while describing another as “a magnificently gruesome memory theater—one that registered our failure to live together with our own transgressions.”

Smith has appeared in five Venice Biennales, and her work is included in museum collections internationally, from the Albertina in Vienna to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Pompidou in Paris, New York’s Museum of Modern Art, and the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.

As Nancy Hass wrote in the New York Times in 2018, Smith “has, over the years, woven from glass, bronze, paper, glitter, steel, lead, clay and thread a vast, all-encompassing universe of enchantment, religious ecstasy and personal mythology.”

Smith got her start in the late 1980s and 1990s. Madeleine Viljoen, curator of the NYPL’s Prints and Spencer Collections, said in an email that “Informed by medical texts like Gray’s Anatomy , the works [Smith] produced during this period focused on the human body, featuring often graphic prints of individual organs, blood vessels, cellular forms, and bodily fluids. Rooted in feminism and unfolding against the backdrop of the AIDS crisis, the works consider flesh and the human body with brutal honesty, viewing them as vessels for trauma, mortality, and political autonomy. By the late 1990s, her work began to explore folklore, mythology and religion from a feminist perspective.”

The NYPL will treat the works quite differently from what one might expect at an art museum.

“We see these materials as art but also materials of study,” said Julie Golia, director of the humanities and social sciences research library, in a video conversation. “Anyone can come in with a library card and spend time with these materials, not behind glass but as a researcher. That kind of access is our special sauce here at 42nd Street.”

The NYPL is a partner in Art Week NYC , a citywide gathering celebrating New York’s leading galleries, institutions, and cultural spaces, organized by ARTnews , Art in America , and Artforum . The inaugural event takes place from November 11–14, 2026.

article_text:
Films and events

Galas

Possible Love

Ga-neung-han sa-rang

Lee Chang-dong’s masterfully directed follow-up to Burning (LFF 2018) finds four strangers’ lives entwined by hidden desires and repressed emotions.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Screening at cinemas around the UK – find out more .

Credits

Director Lee Chang-dong

Screenwriters Lee Chang-dong, Oh Jung-mi

With Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong

South Korea 2026. 164min

Courtesy of Netflix

Language Korean With English subtitles

Introduction

A chance meeting introduces filmmaker Ye-ji to Mi-ok’s family, whose lives have been affected by her husband’s unemployment. They’re perfect subjects for her documentary on workers who have been made redundant, leading them to spend more time in Ye-ji and her husband’s world. But as their connection deepens, the stark contrast between their class and background sees fractures appear in the collaboration, forcing them to confront their marriages and the wider world they all inhabit.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, nudity, and sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

All of a Sudden

Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s delivers an audiaciously tender, transcendent study of humanity through the subtle account of a life-changing encounter.

Hearing

Known for his precise and enigmatic filmmaking, here Lê Bảo crafts a meditative anti-love story revealing fragile connections between humans, sounds and unseen worlds.

Look Back

Spanning more than a decade, Hirokazu Koreeda’s tender coming-of-age story follows two girls who bond over their passion for and dream of becoming manga artists.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Production has wrapped in Los Angeles on the indie drama 1 Am Pacific Time , with Peter Facinelli ( Twilight ) among the leading cast.

The film also stars Alex Vaughan ( Monster: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story ), Billiards U.S. Open Champion Jeanette Lee, and Erica Muñoz ( Grey’s Anatomy ). Filmmaker Brandon DeLany ( Broadway Sandwich ) has written and directed the film.

The film follows a struggling pool hustler, played by Vaughan, who sees a shot at redemption when he wins a large sum of money from the wrong person. He is thrust into a world of dangerous criminals, impossible odds, and life-altering choices, ultimately forced to decide what his own life is worth.

Facinelli plays the Boss, a ruthless figure whose cash ends up in the pool hustler’s hands, and intends to get it back, one way or another.

Watch on Deadline

Muñoz and DeLany, who previously served as producers on the six-time Emmy-nominated PBS series Broadway Sandwich , are producing under their production company, Alexandria Films. Other producers include Meg Saricks, Aaron Champion, and Facinelli.

Facinelli recently starred in and produced The Unbreakable Boy , and co-directed, produced, and starred in On Fire . Muñoz is a Broadway performer known for her breakout role as Mimi in Rent , as well as her leading role in HBO’s Long Gone By . DeLany is known for producing the OWN series Deep Shift .

article_text:
Netflix is swinging the ax — laying off around 1,000 employees, representing 6% of its workforce, in what is its biggest layoff to date.

Most of the layoffs will affect workers in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and HR teams, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in an email to employees Wednesday morning about the layoffs.

“Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety (read it in full below).

A Netflix spokesperson said the company did not have any comment beyond the memo from Sarandos and Peters.

Netflix, the industry’s biggest premium streaming provider with more than 325 million customers globally, has posted double-digit growth in both revenue and profits in recent years. In 2025, the company had $45.2 billion in revenue (up 16%) and net income of $11 billion (up 26%). But investors have been concerned that Netflix’s engagement on a per-user basis slowed in the first half of 2026.

“Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast,” Sarandos and Peters said in the memo. For 2026, Netflix projects revenue of $51.0 billion-$51.4 billion (up 13%-14%) and operating margin of 31.5% (versus 29.5% in 2024).

The co-CEOs continued, “We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” However, they said, “Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors.”

As of the end of 2025, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees.

The last major Netflix layoffs came in 2022, when it axed about 450 staffers following the streamer’s net decline of 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter of that year, its first such drop in more than a decade. The company has made additional smaller cutbacks since then, including letting go several dozen members of its global product team earlier in 2026.

Netflix is scheduled to report third quarter 2026 earnings on Tuesday, Oct. 20, after market close. For the second quarter, the streamer posted earnings in line with Wall Street forecasts , with revenue up 13.4% year-over-year to $12.6 billion and operating margin of 33.4% (down from 34.1% in the year-earlier period). But Netflix issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations, driving the stock price down.

Shares of Netflix were down 1.4% in trading as of 11:30 a.m. ET Wednesday, to $69.45/share, amid a decline in the broader market.

Read the memo from Sarandos and Peters to Netflix staffers:

Team — We wanted to share that we are making a number of organizational changes and, as a result, we’ll be letting go of roughly 6% of our colleagues, with the greatest impact to our product, tech, legal, and HR teams.

Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly. Our top priority today is to support those who are leaving Netflix. The process will vary somewhat by country, but leaders will be connecting with impacted employees soon. If you are leaving, please know that we will support you throughout this transition and make sure you have as much clarity and context as possible. We also want to say thank you. What you’ve built, and the care you brought to Netflix, have made a lasting difference and we will always be grateful.

For the rest of the team, we know you have questions, too. Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources. Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors.

We know changes like this are tough, but let’s stay focused. This is one of the most dynamic times in the history of entertainment — and it’s a moment perfectly suited to a company like ours that’s built at the intersection of technology and entertainment. Now it’s on us to step up and meet the moment, together, like we always do.

Ted and Greg
